lead: A vapour absorption refrigerator gets its cooling from heat instead of shaft work. It keeps the condenser, expansion valve and evaporator of the vapour compression cycle, but replaces the compressor by a liquid loop: an absorber where the refrigerant vapour dissolves in a liquid absorbent, a pump that raises the pressure of that liquid, and a generator where heat drives the refrigerant out again at high pressure. Pumping a liquid takes very little work, so the main input is heat at a moderate temperature: low-pressure steam, hot water, engine exhaust, solar heat. Its COP is lower than a compressor system's, but the heat is often free.
prereq: You need the vapour compression cycle from Vapour compression refrigeration cycle and the Carnot efficiency and COP from the topic Carnot cycle and Carnot's theorem.

blocks.text: In the ammonia-water system, ammonia is the refrigerant and water is the absorbent; water dissolves ammonia readily, more so when cold. The parts are named by what happens in them:

items: Evaporator: liquid ammonia boils at low pressure, taking heat QE from the cold space.
Absorber: the ammonia vapour dissolves in weak solution coming back from the generator, forming strong solution. Dissolving releases heat, so the absorber is cooled with water (heat QA out).
Pump: raises the strong solution to the condenser pressure; a liquid needs little work.
Generator: heat QG boils ammonia vapour out of the strong solution. An analyser and rectifier above it condense the water vapour that comes off with it, so nearly pure ammonia goes on.
Condenser: the ammonia vapour condenses, giving heat QC to the cooling water.
Expansion valve: the liquid ammonia is throttled back to the evaporator pressure.
The weak solution left in the generator returns to the absorber through a solution heat exchanger, where it warms the strong solution going the other way, and a pressure-reducing valve.

blocks.text: The energy balance of the whole plant is QG + QE + Wpump = QC + QA, and COP = QE/(QG + Wpump) ≈ QE/QG.

An absorption plant takes heat at the generator temperature T<sub>G</sub>, takes heat from the cold space at T<sub>E</sub> and rejects heat at the absorber and condenser temperature T<sub>0</sub>, near ambient. Think of it as a reversible heat engine between T<sub>G</sub> and T<sub>0</sub> driving a reversible refrigerator between T<sub>E</sub> and T<sub>0</sub>. The engine turns Q<sub>G</sub> into work Q<sub>G</sub>(1 − T<sub>0</sub>/T<sub>G</sub>), and the refrigerator turns that work into cooling at COP T<sub>E</sub>/(T<sub>0</sub> − T<sub>E</sub>). So
COPmax = (1 − T0/TG) × TE/(T0 − TE), all temperatures in kelvin.

The same result follows from the second law: with no entropy generation, Q<sub>G</sub>/T<sub>G</sub> + Q<sub>E</sub>/T<sub>E</sub> = (Q<sub>G</sub> + Q<sub>E</sub>)/T<sub>0</sub>. The formula has three temperatures; the two-temperature expression T<sub>E</sub>/(T<sub>G</sub> − T<sub>E</sub>) is not the absorption limit. A hotter generator or a colder heat sink raises the COP. Real single-stage plants reach well under half of this limit.

sections.h3: Lithium bromide-water systems and the comparison

blocks.text: In the lithium bromide-water system, water is the refrigerant and LiBr solution the absorbent. Water cannot be cooled below 0 °C without freezing, so these units chill water to about 5 to 7 °C for air conditioning, and their evaporator runs at a deep vacuum. LiBr does not evaporate, so no rectifier is needed. Single-effect LiBr chillers driven by hot water or low-pressure steam have COPs of about 0.7; double-effect units, with a second generator, reach about 1.35 to 1.4. Ammonia-water units are used for cold stores and ice plants below 0 °C.

The Electrolux (three-fluid) refrigerator adds hydrogen to the ammonia-water pair so that the total pressure is the same everywhere; it needs no pump at all, only a small heater, and runs silently in hotel minibars and caravan fridges.

examples.question: An ammonia-water absorption plant has its generator at 120 °C, its condenser and absorber at 30 °C and its evaporator at −10 °C. It must give 10 kW of cooling. Find the ideal COP and the least generator heat. If the actual COP is 0.6, find the generator heat and the total heat rejected to the cooling water (neglect the pump work).
steps: Temperatures in kelvin: T<sub>G</sub> = 393.15 K, T<sub>0</sub> = 303.15 K, T<sub>E</sub> = 263.15 K.
Heat rejected: Q<sub>C</sub> + Q<sub>A</sub> = Q<sub>G</sub> + Q<sub>E</sub> = 16.7 + 10 = 26.7 kW.
examples.answer: COP<sub>max</sub> = 1.51, least generator heat 6.64 kW; with COP 0.6 the generator needs 16.7 kW and the cooling water takes 26.7 kW. The plant reaches 0.6/1.51 = 40% of its ideal COP.

examples.question: A hotel in Chennai wants 100 kW (about 28 TR) of chilled water at 5 °C. A single-effect LiBr chiller (COP 0.7) can run on 90 °C hot water from its diesel generator's exhaust, with cooling water at 35 °C. Find the ideal COP at these temperatures, the heat the chiller needs and the heat rejected. Compare with an electric chiller of COP 4.
steps: Heat needed: Q<sub>G</sub> = 100/0.7 = 142.9 kW of exhaust heat.
Heat rejected to the cooling tower: 100 + 142.9 = 242.9 kW.
Electric chiller: power = 100/4 = 25 kW; heat rejected = 125 kW.
examples.answer: COP<sub>max</sub> = 1.40; the absorption chiller needs 142.9 kW of heat and rejects 242.9 kW, against 25 kW of electricity and 125 kW rejected for the electric chiller. If the exhaust heat would otherwise be wasted, the absorption chiller saves 25 kW of electricity, at the cost of a cooling tower about twice as large.

traps: The ideal absorption COP needs three temperatures: (1 − T<sub>0</sub>/T<sub>G</sub>) × T<sub>E</sub>/(T<sub>0</sub> − T<sub>E</sub>). T<sub>E</sub>/(T<sub>G</sub> − T<sub>E</sub>) is a Carnot refrigerator COP between the evaporator and the generator, which is a different machine.
In ammonia-water the refrigerant is ammonia; in LiBr-water the refrigerant is water. Swapping them is a common slip.
COP below 1 does not mean the plant is badly designed: its input is heat, not work, and the reversible limit at these temperatures is itself only about 1.4 to 1.5.
The heat rejected is Q<sub>G</sub> + Q<sub>E</sub> (plus pump work), shared between the absorber and condenser. Forgetting the absorber's share undersizes the cooling water.
A LiBr-water machine cannot make ice: its refrigerant, water, freezes at 0 °C.

quiz.q: Name the parts of an ammonia-water absorption system that replace the compressor.
quiz.a: The absorber, the solution pump and the generator, with the solution heat exchanger and a valve on the weak-solution return; an analyser and rectifier sit on the generator.

quiz.q: Name the refrigerant and absorbent in the two common absorption systems.
quiz.a: Ammonia-water: ammonia is the refrigerant, water the absorbent. LiBr-water: water is the refrigerant, lithium bromide the absorbent.
Dissolving ammonia in water releases heat, and a cooler solution holds more ammonia. Without cooling, absorption would stop.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the rectifier in an ammonia-water plant, and why does a LiBr plant not need one?
quiz.a: Water evaporates with the ammonia in the generator; the rectifier condenses it out so that dry ammonia reaches the condenser and evaporator. LiBr has no vapour pressure at these temperatures, so only water vapour leaves the generator.

quiz.q: Find the ideal COP of an absorption plant with its generator at 150 °C, condenser and absorber at 35 °C and evaporator at 0 °C.
An absorption plant gives 30 kW of cooling with a generator heat of 50 kW and pump work of 0.5 kW. Find the COP and the heat rejected.
In the first worked example the cooling water warms from 30 °C to 40 °C. How does the ideal COP change, and what does this tell a plant designer?
quiz.a: With T<sub>0</sub> = 313.15 K: (1 − 313.15/393.15) × 263.15/50 = 0.2035 × 5.263 = 1.07, down from 1.51. Cool heat-rejection water matters doubly, because T<sub>0</sub> appears in both the engine and the refrigerator factor.

beyond: Absorption chillers are used in trigeneration plants that make electricity, heat and cooling from one fuel, and in solar-cooling systems. Adsorption chillers use a solid (silica gel or zeolite) instead of a liquid absorbent, and triple-effect LiBr machines push the COP higher with hotter driving heat. Search for "trigeneration absorption chiller", "solar absorption cooling" and "adsorption chiller silica gel".
